facts.label: Sun's gravitational parameter GM (IAU nominal value)

sources.title: IAU 2015 Resolution B3, on recommended nominal conversion constants for selected solar and planetary properties (XXIX General Assembly), PDF on iau.org

facts.notes: Fetched the iau.org PDF on 2026-10-12 and read its text with pdftotext. Table in the 'resolves' section: nominal solar mass parameter (GM)^N_sun = 1.327 124 4 × 10^20 m^3 s^-2. The resolution says the nominal values 'are by definition exact and are expressed in SI units' and 'should be understood as conversion factors only — chosen to be close to the current best estimates ... not as the true solar ... properties'. Endnote 1: the value is 'adopted as an exact number, given with a precision within which its TCB and TDB values agree'. So it is a standard value, not a measurement, but it matches the measured GM of the Sun to all 8 figures shown, which is far more precise than this page needs. The same table gives Earth's nominal GM, 3.986 004 × 10^14 m^3 s^-2, which matches the existing earth_gm fact. Existing facts cite this resolution as arXiv:1510.07674; that copy was not re-fetched here. Use: input for the solar escape speed (sun_escape_speed_at_1au).
facts.quote: Table cell: "(GM)^N_sun = 1.327 124 4 × 10^20 m3 s−2" (pdftotext renders the Sun symbol as '1': "1(GM)N = 1.327 124 4 × 1020 m3 s−2"); text: "the nominal values RN, SN, LN, TeffN, and (GM)N, be used, respectively, which are by definition exact and are expressed in SI units."

facts.label: Astronomical unit (au)
facts.display: About 149.6 million km (exactly 149,597,870,700 m by definition)

sources.title: IAU 2012 Resolution B2, on the re-definition of the astronomical unit of length (XXVIII General Assembly), English PDF on the IAU's archived site
IAU 2015 Resolution B3, endnote 4, restating the 2012 definition (iau.org PDF)

facts.notes: Fetched both PDFs on 2026-10-12 and read them with pdftotext. 2012 B2, 'recommends' clause 1, defines the au as exactly 149 597 870 700 m. 2015 B3 endnote 4 says: 'Resolution B2 of the XXVIII General Assembly of the IAU in 2012 defined the astronomical unit to be a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly.' The au is a defined unit close to Earth's average distance from the Sun. It is not Earth's actual distance on a given day, which varies by about ±1.7% over a year (eccentricity about 0.017; not verified here). That would shift the solar escape speed by less than 1%. The iau.org 'List of Resolutions' page now links the 2012 resolutions only in French (via Google Drive). The English text came from the IAU's archived static site at iauarchive.eso.org, the old www.iau.org/static/resolutions/ path, which now returns 404.

facts.label: Speed needed to escape the Sun from Earth's distance (1 au)
facts.display: About 42.1 km/s, measured relative to the Sun

sources.title: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 (GM of the Sun), iau.org PDF
IAU 2012 Resolution B2 (astronomical unit), IAU archive PDF

facts.notes: Arithmetic: v = sqrt(2 GM_sun / au) = sqrt(2 × 1.3271244e20 / 1.495978707e11) = sqrt(1.7742557e9 m^2/s^2) = 42,121.9 m/s, about 42.1 km/s. Check: the circular orbit speed at 1 au, sqrt(GM_sun / au) = 29,785 m/s, is Earth's familiar mean orbital speed of about 29.8 km/s, and escape speed is sqrt(2) times it. What it ignores: (1) It is measured relative to the Sun, not Earth. Earth already moves at about 29.8 km/s, so once clear of Earth's gravity a throw along Earth's motion needs only about 12.3 km/s more, and a throw straight against it needs about 71.9 km/s. (2) Earth's own pull: from the ground, in the best direction, the speed needed is about sqrt(12.34^2 + 11.19^2), roughly 16.7 km/s, using the existing earth_escape_velocity_surface fact. This ignores air, Earth's spin and the other planets. (3) The other planets' pulls. (4) Relativity, which is negligible: 42 km/s is about 0.014% of light speed. For the page's threshold: 3,000 km/s is about 70 times this speed, so none of these corrections matter there. Rough check, an estimate rather than a sourced figure: at 3,000 km/s the Sun's pull bends a path that never comes closer than 1 au by at most about 2 GM_sun / (b v^2) = 2 × 1.327e20 / (1.496e11 × 9e12), about 2 × 10^-4 rad (0.01°). It also slows the object by about 0.01%. So 'flies off in a straight line' holds, unless it is aimed close to the Sun.
facts.quote: Derived; no fetched page carries this number. Inputs as quoted: "(GM)^N_sun = 1.327 124 4 × 10^20 m3 s−2" (IAU 2015 B3) and "a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly" (IAU 2012 B2).

facts.label: Speed needed to escape the Milky Way from the Sun's position
facts.display: About 530 km/s; published estimates run from 445 to 580 km/s

sources.title: Piffl et al. (2014) The RAVE survey: the Galactic escape speed and the mass of the Milky Way, A&A 562, A91; arXiv abstract page
Piffl et al. (2014), arXiv v3 PDF (abstract on p. 1)
Piffl et al. (2014), published abstract on Macquarie University's research portal (A&A 562, A91, DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201322531)
Deason et al. (2019) The local high velocity tail and the Galactic escape speed, MNRAS 485, 3514-3526; arXiv abstract page
Monari et al. (2018) The escape speed curve of the Galaxy obtained from Gaia DR2 implies a heavy Milky Way, A&A 616, L9; arXiv abstract page
Koppelman & Helmi (2021) Determination of the escape velocity of the Milky Way using a proper motion selected halo sample, A&A 649, A136; arXiv abstract page
Necib & Lin (2022) Substructure at High Speed. II. The Local Escape Velocity and Milky Way Mass with Gaia eDR3, ApJ 926, 189; Caltech repository record
Milky Way Mass Through Escape Velocity Curve from LAMOST K Giants (2025 preprint, arXiv:2510.18227)

facts.notes: All pages fetched 2026-10-12. Measurements: (1) Piffl et al. 2014, from RAVE survey stars: 533 (+54, -41) km/s at 90% confidence, plus a 4% systematic uncertainty. Here 'escape' means reaching three virial radii (3 R340). Wording discrepancy: the arXiv listing's abstract says '5% systematic'. That text is left over from v1, which gave 537 (+59, -43). The v3 PDF abstract and the published abstract both say 4%, so 4% is used. (2) Deason et al. 2019, from Gaia DR2 data plus cosmological simulations: 528 (+24, -25) km/s at 8.3 kpc from the Galactic centre, with the boundary at 2 r200. The abstract does not say what confidence level these errors are. (3) Monari et al. 2018, from Gaia DR2 (about 2,850 counter-rotating halo stars): 580 ± 63 km/s, boundary at three virial radii. It shares authors (Piffl, Steinmetz) and method with (1), so it is not counted as independent. (4) Koppelman & Helmi 2021, from Gaia (about 10^7 halo stars, sideways motions only): 497 ± 8 km/s. The authors call this 'most likely biased low, our best guess is by 10%' and say the true value 'most likely is closer to 550 km/s'. (5) Necib & Lin 2022, from Gaia eDR3 with a multi-component fit: 445 (+25, -8) km/s with two components (preferred), and 472 (+17, -12) km/s with one. Their arXiv v1 used Gaia DR2 and gave 484.6 (+17.8, -7.4); the published eDR3 value is used here. (6) 2025 LAMOST K-giant preprint, using Gaia DR3: 523.74 (+12.83, -13.47) km/s. The arXiv page shows no journal reference. Why 'verified': (1) and (2) come from different surveys (RAVE versus Gaia), teams and methods, and they agree within their errors (533 versus 528). (6) also agrees. Value used: 530 km/s, rounding (1) and (2). Range: the published central values run from 445 km/s (Necib & Lin 2022) to 580 km/s (Monari 2018). With error bars the span is about 437 to 643 km/s. Newer Gaia analyses tend to sit lower, at 445 to 525 km/s. The spread comes from how the tail of the fastest stars is modelled and from where 'escape' is set. The Galaxy has no sharp edge, so 'escape' means reaching a chosen far radius (3 R340 or 2 r200), and the Local Group (Andromeda) is ignored. What it ignores for the page: the speed is relative to the Galaxy's centre, not to the Sun or Earth. The papers assume the Sun circles the Galaxy at 230 to 240 km/s (Necib & Lin 230 ± 10, Koppelman & Helmi 232.8, Monari 240). So a throw along the Sun's orbit needs roughly 300 km/s relative to the Sun, and one straight against it roughly 765 km/s. The Sun's and Earth's pulls add only a little. These are rough figures, not sourced. A 3,000 km/s throw is about 6 times 530 km/s, and about 4 times even the worst case against the Sun's motion. So in this model it leaves the Galaxy in any direction, unless it hits something. Rough estimate, not sourced: the Galaxy's pull bends such a path by roughly (v_c / v)^2 ≈ (235/3000)^2 ≈ 0.006 rad, times a factor of a few, about a degree at most.
facts.quote: Piffl et al. (v3 PDF and published abstract): "Our best estimate of the local Galactic escape speed, which we define as the minimum speed required to reach three virial radii R340, is 533+54−41 km s−1 (90% confidence) with an additional 4% systematic uncertainty"; Deason et al.: "After applying our methodology to the Gaia data, we find a local (r_0=8.3 kpc) escape speed of v_esc(r_0) = 528(+24,-25) km/s."

problems: Number, unit and status check out. I fetched the iau.org PDF (HTTP 200) and ran pdftotext on it. The SOLAR CONVERSION CONSTANTS table reads '1(GM)N = 1.327 124 4 × 10^20 m3 s−2'. Recommends 1 says the nominal values 'are by definition exact and are expressed in SI units' and 'should be understood as conversion factors only — chosen to be close to the current best estimates (see table below) — not as the true solar properties.' 'official' is the right status for an IAU resolution constant.

Wrong place cited: the 'adopted as an exact number, given with a precision within which its TCB and TDB values agree' sentence is in the Explanation section, item 1, not 'Endnote 1'. Endnote 1 in the PDF's Notes is about v sin i and stellar rotation periods.

Wrong description of the pdftotext output: the Sun symbol is not rendered as '1', it is dropped. The '1' is a literal part of the table ('1 nominal unit = ...'). The planetary rows read '1 (GM)NE = 3.986 004 × 10^14' the same way.

Unsupported claim in the notes: 'it matches the measured GM of the Sun to all 8 figures shown'. No fetched page carries a measured GM_sun to compare against. The PDF says only that the value was 'chosen to be close to the current best estimates' and is given to the precision within which its TCB and TDB values agree. Reword, or cite IAU 2009 / Luzum et al. 2011.

Integration warning, not a fact error: no existing fact uses the status 'official'. build-data.py's RANK has no 'official', so status() ranks it 9, weaker than everything. A page row keyed on sun_gm plus a derived fact would then be labelled 'official' instead of 'derived'. app.html's STATUS_LABEL and badge CSS also lack it. Facts from the same resolution (earth_gm, iau_nominal_solar_radius) use 'verified'. The builder must add 'official' to RANK, STATUS_LABEL and the CSS, or use 'verified' for consistency.

Resolution B2 is 'on the re-definition of the astronomical unit of length', and recommends 1 reads exactly as quoted: 'that the astronomical unit be re-defined to be a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly, in agreement with the value adopted in IAU 2009 Resolution B2,'. I redid the arithmetic. 2 × 1.3271244e20 / 149597870700 = 1.77425573e9 m^2/s^2, and its square root is 42,121.9 m/s, so value_si 42122 is right. Circular speed sqrt(GM/au) = 29,784.7 m/s. Along Earth's motion: 42,121.9 − 29,784.7 = 12,337 m/s. Against it: 71,907 m/s. From the ground, sqrt(12,337^2 + 11,186^2) = 16,653 m/s, about 16.7 km/s. 42.1 km/s is 0.0141% of c. 3,000 km/s is 71 times this speed. The bend, 2GM/(b v^2) with b = 1 au and v = 3e6 m/s, is 1.97e-4 rad = 0.011°. The slow-down, (GM/au)/v^2, is 9.9e-5, about 0.01%. All as stated. 'derived' is the right status, and both input URLs were fetched.

Minor: 'Earth's familiar mean orbital speed of about 29.8 km/s' is unsourced. It is only a sanity check, but the NASA Earth Fact Sheet already cited in final-environment.json gives the mean orbital velocity and could be cited.

Status stronger than the evidence. The README's status rule says 'verified is reserved for numbers as the source states them'. value_si 530 km/s appears on no source; it is the researcher's rounding of 533 and 528. The measurements also disagree beyond their stated errors: Necib & Lin 2022 give 445 +25/−8, so at most 470; Deason gives at least 503 and Piffl at least 492. The house precedent for a central value picked from disagreeing published values is 'disputed' (energy_chicxulub_impact, the asteroid fact the task points to, plus energy_tunguska_1908, energy_tsar_bomba_yield and statue_of_liberty_*). Use 'disputed', or at least 'reported', not 'verified'.

The '2025 preprint' (arXiv:2510.18227) is a published paper. Its arXiv page's comments field reads '13 pages, 8 figures, published in ApJ' and links DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/adf2a4. Crossref gives Wu, Li, Huang, Xue & Zhao, ApJ 990, 182 (2025). The page also lists the authors (Yin Wu, Haining Li, Yang Huang, Xiang-Xiang Xue, Gang Zhao). So the note and the gap saying 'no journal reference ... authors were not recorded' are wrong. Only the formal jref field is empty.

Two claims rest on a page that is not cited: Necib & Lin's '230 ± 10' km/s circular speed, and their 'arXiv v1 used Gaia DR2 and gave 484.6 (+17.8, -7.4)'. Neither is on the cited Caltech record, whose published abstract gives no circular speed. Both are on the arXiv v1 abstract page (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02211v1, which I fetched). Add it as a source.
Deason et al.: the cited abstract says only '6-dimensional Gaia data', not 'Gaia DR2'. The DR2 label is not supported by the cited page.

Everything else checks out on the fetched pages. arXiv 1309.4293 abstract: 533 +54/−41 (90% confidence), '5% systematic'. The v1 abstract page confirms 537 +59/−43 and 5% for v1. v3 PDF abstract: 533 +54/−41 '(90% confidence) with an additional 4% systematic uncertainty'. Macquarie record: the same with a comma after '(90% confidence)', A&A 562, A91, DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201322531. Deason: 528(+24,−25) at r_0 = 8.3 kpc, boundary 2 r_200, no confidence level stated; Crossref gives MNRAS 485(3), 3514–3526. Monari: 580 ± 63, about 2,850 counter-rotating halo stars, three virial radii, 240 km/s (and 228 km/s in the ΛCDM case). Koppelman & Helmi: 497 +8/−8, 'most likely biased low, our best guess is by 10%', 'closer to 550 km/s', about 10^7 halo stars, v_c = 232.8 km/s. Necib & Lin (Caltech): 445 +25/−8 for two components (preferred), 472 +17/−12 for one, Gaia eDR3, ApJ 926, 189. Wu et al.: 523.74 +12.83/−13.47. Range 445–580 (central values) and 437–643 (with errors) recomputed correctly. 530 − 235 ≈ 295 and 530 + 235 = 765 are correct.
Minor: the 'span with error bars' (437–643) mixes intervals. Piffl's are 90% confidence; the others are unstated or probably 1σ. Say so if the page shows it.
Minor: 'newer Gaia analyses tend to sit lower, at 445 to 525 km/s' counts Koppelman & Helmi's raw 497, although the authors themselves put the true value near 550.
